doc.title: Slide Hampton interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003

title: Keeping a big band together
summary: Good musicians have many projects, so personnel changes constantly, as with the trombone album.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: Well it sounds like your calendar and your plate remains full.

I worked so much in the last few months. I was working so much that I couldn’t get to practice or anything. Now I’m able to practice. I’m practicing and writing, because I have these things coming up where I have to do all my own music and all of that for the radio and things like that. So I’m getting a chance right now, all day long I’m practicing and writing. And it’s just a wonderful feeling.
Is it hard to keep a big band fairly consistent from a personnel standpoint?

Almost impossible. When you have good musicians they’re always doing a lot of other things. So you can never keep a band with all the same guys anymore. There was a time when you could do that. But not now. All good musicians have a lot of projects of their own that they’re doing, so you get them once in a while but not very often.
It must be hard to just mount one concert.
To get a rehearsal in and scheduling.

It’s a job. When we did the trombone album, the trombone CD, we did that one thing, but we could never have that same group again. But we had good guys after that too, guys that weren’t on the CD. And when we did the trombone thing recently at the Blue Note with Bobby Burgess and Bill Watrous you know, those guys and Benny Powell, they love to work together so they’ll just about do anything they can to get to work in that group © Fillius Jazz Archive -24-
because they loved being there so much. But in general when you’ve got a group like that it’s hard to get that group together more than once. There always will be some change in there.
